1	---
2	title: "Self-Improving Agents Are Event-Sourced"
3	description: "An agent improves when its next run can see what the last run did and what happened after. That is a storage problem before it is a model problem, and the storage is an append-only event log that proxies your systems of record."
4	date: 2026-07-28
5	author: Burak Emre Kabakcı
6	authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba
7	tags: [architecture, agents, memory, event-sourcing]
8	cover: /design/prim-channels.webp
9	draft: false
10	---
11	
12	import { TruthProxyDiagram } from "../../components/blog/TruthProxyDiagram";
13	import { MemberResolutionDiagram } from "../../components/blog/MemberResolutionDiagram";
14	
15	Everyone wants self-improving agents, and the fashionable answers are model-side: reflection loops, fine-tuning, memory frameworks with philosophical names. I think the answer is boring. It is event sourcing. An agent improves when its next run can see what the last run did, what a human said about it, and what happened after. That is a storage problem before it is a model problem.
16	
17	The storage cannot be another system of record, though. The truth already has homes. Slack owns the conversation, Stripe owns the payment, the warehouse owns revenue, and any product that asks you to move them becomes the thing you migrate away from in two years. So we built a proxy instead. Lobu's memory is an append-only event log that mirrors the systems you already run. The sources keep the truth. The log keeps the observations, one place every agent reads and writes, with permissions compiled into every query.
18	
19	<TruthProxyDiagram />
20	
21	## Never update, never delete
22	
23	Every row in the log is an observation: a Slack thread a feed pulled, a payment webhook, a note an agent saved. The comment on the table states the contract: "Never DELETE; supersede with a tombstone row that points at the original." A database trigger blocks deletes outright. Updates don't exist either. Changing a fact means appending a new event that points at the one it replaces, and the read view masks every superseded row. Roughly three quarters of the rows in our production store are superseded. That sounds wasteful right up until you need to know what the agent believed on Tuesday.
24	
25	Sync follows the same discipline. A feed pulls a thread or a contact. Unchanged items write nothing, changed items write a new observation that supersedes the old one. And the log is curated, not a data lake: raw chat transcripts deliberately stay out of it, and a message worth remembering gets promoted into an event.
26	
27	The discipline exists because agents are prolific writers and unreliable editors. Give a fleet of agents UPDATE and you will spend incident reviews reconstructing what got clobbered. Give them supersession and every mistake is one pointer away from undone. Provenance stops being a feature. It is the storage format.
28	
29	## The session was the prototype
30	
31	We did not invent this shape. We adopted it from the harness we run. Lobu's agent runtime is [pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono), Mario Zechner's coding-agent harness, and a pi session is an append-only JSONL file: user turns, assistant turns, tool results, one entry after another, never edited in place. Replay the file and you get the agent back. The best coding agents converged on this because it makes a run resumable, auditable, and forkable, and I think it is a large part of why the harness works as well as it does.
32	
33	Lobu runs the same shape one level up. The organization gets one log, and the agent's session meets it everywhere. A Behavior fires and the triggering event arrives in the session as a message, JSON included. The agent pulls more context and the events come back as tool results. A colleague's Slack message, an approval decision, another agent's saved note: all of it reaches the agent the same way, as one more entry in a stream it can read. And everything the agent does flows the other way, back into the log, stamped with the run that did it. Collaboration is not a feature we bolted on. It is what a shared log does. Two agents cooperate the same way two services in an event-sourced system do: one writes, the other reacts.
34	
35	## The entities we ship
36	
37	Entities live next to the log: companies, deals, goals, whatever your config declares. Agents query them by name. An unknown table in an agent's SQL resolves as an entity type, so `SELECT name FROM company` just works, scoped to your org and your permissions. A few types ship with the platform, prefixed with `$`, and they do the governance work.
38	
39	`$member` is a person. The same human shows up as a Slack user id, an email address, a web login. Each one is an identity claim in a single table, and the claims resolve onto one member entity. Sign in with an identity a sync already saw and the claim moves onto your member. Two members claiming the same identity is a conflict we refuse to guess about: that's two humans and one Slack id, and nothing merges. Merging is an explicit operation, logged and reversible, and the log itself is never rewritten.
40	
41	<MemberResolutionDiagram />
42	
43	`$resource` is the access-control anchor. A Slack channel and a GitHub repo are the same kind of thing: a unit of access, with membership edges synced from the source. An agent recalls a channel's history only for someone whose member entity is a member of that channel. When the membership sync goes stale, the gate fails closed. A stalled sync hides data. It does not leak it.
44	
45	Metrics are the deliberate exception, because a metric should not be a row anyone edits. A metric is a declared definition on an entity type: measures over event sets, with named segments, compiled into the same org-scoped SQL every other read uses. Declare `asset.spend` once and the dashboard sparkline, the agent's answer, and your goal tracking compute the same number from the same events. Even the dashboard is event-sourced: lifecycle changes are themselves events, and the stats fold over them.
46	
47	## Who holds the keys
48	
49	Everything enters and leaves through connectors. Feeds pull data in on a schedule or receive webhooks, actions push changes out. Auth is whatever the source demands: managed OAuth, your own OAuth app, API keys, org-level app installs, a paired browser extension riding a session you're already signed into, or a connector pinned to a specific device. With managed OAuth the client secret and refresh token never leave our cloud; your instance receives an access token and its expiry, nothing more. At rest, credentials are AES-256-GCM encrypted and scoped per organization.
50	
51	The invariant we hold hardest: an agent worker never sees a real credential. Workers get placeholder tokens. A proxy at the network edge swaps the placeholder for the real value as the request leaves the box, and the worker's egress is forced through that proxy, so the secret only ever exists outside the sandbox. The one exception is deliberate: a connection pinned to your own device runs with that device's credentials, because that is exactly what you authorized when you bound it.
52	
53	Privacy rides the same read path as everything else. A connection backed by a personal OAuth login is forced private, enforced by a database trigger, so your Gmail cannot surface in a coworker's recall no matter what an agent asks.
54	
55	## Notifications are events with an envelope
56	
57	Consequential writes are where most agent platforms bolt on an approval queue. Ours is the log again. When an agent wants to do something gated, one transaction writes a pending run and a pending approval event. The event carries an interaction envelope: a type, a status, the proposed input, and the JSON schema describing that input. The schema is why the card is interactive. The web app feeds it into a form, so the reviewer can edit the proposed arguments before approving. The same card goes to Slack with Approve and Reject buttons, and both paths call the same tool underneath.
58	
59	![The approval timeline in the Lobu app: every card is an event, and the status chip is live state](/blog/approval-timeline.png)
60	
61	The decision is a supersession, of course. Approving inserts a new event that points at the pending one, stamped with the reviewer, so the person who authorized the run owns its whole outcome in the audit trail. The worker's claim query only ever selects approved work, which makes an unapproved action structurally unclaimable: there is no code path by which it runs. When the action finishes, the outcome supersedes again, carrying the output or the error.
62	
63	![One action's full record: requested by an MCP client, approved by a human, the proposed input, and the error it returned](/blog/approval-envelope.png)
64	
65	One detail I like: approvals nobody decides expire after seven days, and expired is a distinct status from rejected. An agent must not learn silence as disapproval.
66	
67	## The loop is the improvement
68	
69	Put it together and self-improvement stops being mystical. Every action lands in the log with run provenance. The outcome lands later, as more events. The approvals, the rejections, the edited inputs, the guidance an admin writes: all of it lands too, attributed and permanent, and the next run reads it. The model in the loop gets better a few times a year, when a lab ships. The agent gets better every day, because the substrate underneath it remembers.
70	
71	We could market that substrate as the single source of truth for agents. It isn't, and it shouldn't be. The truth stays in the systems that own it. The log keeps what was observed, who may see it, and what every agent did about it. That is the whole trick.
72	
73	Start with the [docs](/getting-started/), or read how the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/) works.
74

# Blog voice

How posts under `src/content/blog/` should read. Reference example: `shopifys-aquifer-in-the-open.mdx`.

The target is the voice of Shopify's "Under the River" engineering post, written in first person. Confident, plain, technical without posturing. Sounds like an engineer explaining a real opinion to peers, not a marketing page and not an essay.

## Do

- **Open with an opinion, not a summary.** Take a position in the first two paragraphs. Disagree with something. If the post only restates a source, it has no reason to exist.
- **Short declarative sentences, varied with longer ones.** Let a fragment land for emphasis: "That is the easy version." "A product does."
- **Repeat the key noun** instead of reaching for synonyms. "The corpus", "the memory", "the session". Repetition builds the through-line.
- **Open each section with a constraint or fact, then pivot to the insight.**
- **First person.** "We made the same bet." "I wrote about that split in..." Own the claim.
- **Argue with specifics.** Name the table, the mechanism, the real difference. Vague beats nothing, specific beats vague.
- **Plain, slightly declarative headers.** Statements or mild antithesis: "The corpus is the asset. The conversation isn't." Not clever, not cute.

## Don't

- **No em dashes.** Hard rule for all landing copy. Use periods, commas, or parentheses. This also forces the staccato rhythm we want.
- **No three-beat marketing chants.** "Your agent. Your data. Your servers." is the single clearest AI tell. Kill it on sight.
- **No rhetorical questions** as a transition ("So why store the noise?").
- **No stacked tricolons** or relentless "not X, but Y" balance in every paragraph. One antithesis per stretch, not five.
- **No clever-for-clever's-sake** word pairs ("noise vs signal", "same goal, different cut", "strictly harder"). They read as filler.
- **No hedging AI filler:** "it's worth noting", "on one hand / on the other", "in today's world".
- **Don't paraphrase the source** section by section. Engage two or three points with depth instead of touring all of them.

## Shape

- Comparison or opinion posts: roughly 600 to 700 words.
- 3 to 5 sentences per paragraph, rarely longer.
- Quote a source verbatim when it sharpens the point, but keep quotes short.

## The test

Read it out loud. If a line sounds like a slide deck or a press release, rewrite it. If it sounds like you talking, keep it.

1	---
2	title: "Shopify's Aquifer, in the Open"
3	description: "Shopify treats an agent's corpus as the compounding asset. Lobu keeps the signal—not the chat—and makes that architecture work across companies."
4	date: 2026-05-29
5	author: Burak Emre Kabakcı
6	authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba
7	tags: [architecture, agents, memory]
8	cover: /design/tabfig-memory.webp
9	draft: false
10	---
11	
12	Shopify published [Under the River](https://shopify.engineering/under-the-river), the writeup of the substrate they built so agents could become real participants in how they ship code. Read past the Slack bot and there's a bet. They state it plainly: "the corpus is the compounding asset; the privacy of an agent thread is a disadvantage."
13	
14	We made the same bet. An agent that only helps the person at the keyboard is autocomplete. An agent that learns from everyone is infrastructure. The disagreement is narrow, and it is about what you write down.
15	
16	## The corpus is the asset. The conversation isn't.
17	
18	River is public by default. The threads pile up in Slack, stay searchable, and the patterns get fed back into River's skills later. The corpus is the chat. The signal gets pulled out after the fact.
19	
20	We don't keep the chat. We keep what the chat was about. Every interaction becomes an event in an append-only log: structured, embedded, searchable. Extraction happens once, at write time, instead of every time you read. The conversation is scaffolding. The event is the thing that lasts.
21	
22	This is the warehouse, not the notebook. I wrote about that split in [Filesystem vs Database for Agent Memory](/blog/filesystem-vs-database-agent-memory/). The filesystem is where the agent thinks. The memory layer is where the company remembers.
23	
24	Shopify are halfway here. River writes its own sessions to a `river_sessions` table. We have a table too. The difference is that ours is not a log bolted onto one agent. In Lobu the events log is the platform. Every agent reads it and writes it. They share one memory. A new agent inherits the whole history instead of starting on an empty table.
25	
26	## One memory. Everyone.
27	
28	This is what turns a fast assistant into a useful one. You ask, and it already knows. The colleague who hit the same wall last week. The decision made in another channel. The customer a sales thread mentioned. One agent, one company memory, and it gets denser every day the company shows up.
29	
30	## One company is the easy version
31	
32	Under the River never says the word "organization." It doesn't have to. Everything lives inside Shopify. One company, one corpus, shared by default.
33	
34	That is the easy version. The hard one is many companies at once. The memory stays separate per org. The credentials per tenant. All on the same machines, and no org's agent ever touches another's data. That is the real work, and it is what Lobu is built around. Each org gets its own memory that compounds, on shared infrastructure, walled off from the rest. A single company never has to solve this. A product does.
35	
36	## Keep the agent away from the secrets
37	
38	Their first lesson is to keep the harness out of the sandbox. The agent loop should not live where the code runs, so a bad turn has a small blast radius. We agree, and we draw a second line. The worker never holds a real secret. A proxy sits in front of it and swaps placeholder tokens for the real ones only as a request leaves the box. The agent uses credentials it never sees and can never leak.
39	
40	## The difference
41	
42	River runs inside Shopify and that is where it stays. Lobu is the version you run yourself. Same memory, same agent everyone talks to, except the database stays under your control and model traffic follows the providers you configure. The only thing we really had to add is the part where it holds up for many companies on one install, not one company that owns the whole place.
43	
44	Start with the [docs](/getting-started/), or read how the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/) works.
45

---
title: "Self-Improving Agents Are Event-Sourced"
description: "The interesting part of a self-improving agent isn't the model. It's that the next run can see what the last run did, which is a storage problem with a boring, well-understood answer."
date: 2026-07-28
author: Burak Emre Kabakcı
authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba
tags: [architecture, agents, memory, event-sourcing]
cover: /design/prim-channels.webp
draft: false
---

import { TruthProxyDiagram } from "../../components/blog/TruthProxyDiagram";

Most of the proposals I see for self-improving agents are model-side: reflection loops, fine-tuning on your own traces, memory frameworks with names borrowed from cognitive science. I've come round to a much more boring answer. An agent improves when its next run can see what the last run did, what a human said about it, and what happened afterwards. That's a storage problem, and event sourcing solved it a decade before anyone was building agents.

The catch is that this storage can't be another system of record. The truth already has homes. Slack owns the conversation, Stripe owns the payment, the warehouse owns revenue, and any product that asks you to move them becomes the thing you migrate off in two years. So the log we built for Lobu is a proxy: an append-only record of observations about systems we don't own. The sources keep the truth. The log keeps what was seen, who may see it, and what every agent did about it.

<TruthProxyDiagram />

## The database refuses to forget

Every row is an observation: a Slack thread a feed pulled, a payment webhook, a note an agent saved. Changing a fact means appending a new row that points at the one it replaces, via `supersedes_event_id`, and the read view masks anything that's been superseded. There is no UPDATE path and no DELETE path.

That was a convention for a long time, written in a `COMMENT ON TABLE` and in our AGENTS.md, which is to say it was enforced by nothing at all. Any psql session or admin tool could still wipe rows. So it became a trigger:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.events_block_direct_delete()
  RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  IF pg_trigger_depth() > 1 THEN
    RETURN OLD; -- FK cascade (org delete) or another trigger's cleanup
  END IF;
  IF current_setting('lobu.allow_event_delete', true) = 'on' THEN
    RETURN OLD; -- sanctioned maintenance, transaction-scoped
  END IF;
  RAISE EXCEPTION
    'events is append-only: DELETE of event % blocked.',
    OLD.id
    USING ERRCODE = 'check_violation';
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
```

The two escape hatches are the interesting part. `pg_trigger_depth() > 1` lets a foreign-key cascade through, because deleting an organization genuinely does need to sweep its events, and cascaded deletes run nested inside the RI system trigger while a direct `DELETE FROM events` fires at depth 1. The second is an opt-in for sanctioned maintenance, and it uses `SET LOCAL` specifically so a pooled connection can't leak the bypass into somebody else's later query. TRUNCATE and DROP TABLE don't fire row-level delete triggers at all, so test teardown was unaffected.

I like this pattern more than I expected to. The invariant stops being something you remember and starts being something the database enforces on everyone, including future me at 2am.

The cost is real: our current view is 222,611 rows, of which 27,108 exist only to supersede an earlier row. You're paying storage to keep versions nobody is going to read. That sounds wasteful right up until the first time somebody asks what the agent believed on Tuesday.

## The coding-agent harness got there first

We didn't invent this shape, and I want to be clear about where it came from. Lobu's agent runtime is [pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono), Mario Zechner's coding-agent harness, and a pi session is an append-only JSONL file. User turn, assistant turn, tool result, one entry after another, never edited in place. Replay the file and you get the agent back.

I don't think that's a coincidence. The good coding agents converged on append-only session files because it's what makes a run resumable, auditable, and forkable, and those three properties are most of what makes the harness feel reliable.

So Lobu runs the same shape one level up. Instead of one file per session, the organization gets one log, and the session meets it everywhere: a Behavior fires and the triggering event arrives in the session as a message, the agent asks for more context and events come back as tool results, and everything the agent does flows back into the log stamped with the run that did it.

The part I didn't anticipate is that this makes collaboration fall out for free. Two agents cooperate the same way two services in any event-sourced system do. One writes, the other reacts. We never built a multi-agent feature; we just had a shared log and stopped needing one.

## Approvals are just supersession

The place this paid off most is the bit every agent platform ends up bolting on: human approval for consequential writes.

Ours is the same log. When an agent wants to do something gated, one transaction writes a pending run and a pending approval event. Approving doesn't update that event, it appends a new one pointing at it, stamped with whoever decided. The action's outcome supersedes again later, carrying the output or the error.

![One action's full record: requested by an MCP client, approved by a human, the proposed input, and the error it returned](/blog/approval-envelope.png)

Two consequences I'd flag. The worker's claim query only ever selects approved work, so an unapproved action isn't blocked by a check somewhere, it's structurally unclaimable: there's no code path by which it runs. And approvals nobody decides expire after seven days, with expired kept as a status distinct from rejected, because an agent should never get to learn that silence means disapproval.

## Why this is the improvement

None of the above is clever. That's the point I'd like to land. Every action lands in the log with run provenance, the outcome lands later as more events, and the approvals, rejections, edited inputs and guidance an admin writes all land too, attributed and permanent. The next run reads them.

The model in the loop gets better a few times a year, when a lab ships something. The agent gets better every week, because the substrate underneath it remembers. I'd rather own the second one.

The temptation is to market a log like this as the single source of truth for agents. It isn't, and it shouldn't be, and I think products that make that pitch are quietly asking you to migrate onto them. The truth stays in the systems that own it.

Start with the [docs](/getting-started/), or read how the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/) works.

# Active Graph Architecture

## Event Sourcing Fundamentals

Active Graph implements a classical event-sourced architecture where the append-only log serves as the system's source of truth. The framework materializes a working graph as a deterministic projection of this immutable event history.

**Key architectural principle:** "The graph is the projection of the event log; every mutation is an event."

## The Event Log

The system maintains an append-only event log containing all mutations. Every behavior fires in response to events and produces additional events, creating an ordered trace. The log persists in SQLite (default) or Postgres via the `EventStore` protocol. There is no deletion—only appending occurs.

Event types are fixed by the framework (lifecycle, graph mutations, behavior execution, LLM calls, patches, approvals) while applications emit custom event types as needed.

## The Graph and Its Relation to Events

The materialized graph comprises typed objects and relations. Rather than serving as the primary record, it functions as a queryable projection. The framework describes this relationship: "Every mutation is an event; the trace is the audit trail."

The `GraphStore` protocol makes the materialized projection pluggable. The default in-memory implementation exists alongside external backends like FalkorDB for traversable Cypher queries.

## Replay Mechanism

Active Graph supports deterministic replay from the event log. The framework distinguishes between strict mode (re-fires every behavior, fails on divergence) and permissive mode (reconstructs state without re-firing). Critically, LLM replay caching makes forking inexpensive by avoiding redundant provider calls across shared event prefixes.

## Versioning and Forking

Rather than git-like branching, Active Graph enables "fork-and-diff" capabilities: branch any run at any historical event into an independent fork, reconfigure it, and structurally diff results against the parent. This hypothesis-testing primitive is described as "the framework's most differentiated capability."

No tombstone or supersession mechanism is mentioned—the model relies on event append-only semantics exclusively.

All three verified. Here's what I'd add, and why each earns its place.

## 1. The projection is a real view, not a metaphor

Your post says "the read view masks anything that's been superseded," which is vague. It's an actual SQL view whose entire definition is one `NOT EXISTS`:

```sql
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM public.events newer
  WHERE newer.supersedes_event_id = e.id
)
```

That's the whole mechanism. Current state is a query, not a stored thing. Yohei states this as a law — *"the graph is the projection of the event log"* — and you have the same property but never claim it. Worth two sentences plus that snippet, because it makes the append-only claim structural instead of a policy you promise to follow.

## 2. What we haven't built (forking)

I checked rather than trusting the memory note. `grep -rn "fork"` across the server source returns exactly one hit, and it's a comment in a test about re-delivery. There is no fork. There's also no event-log replay: every "replay" in the codebase is either migration idempotency or chat-history rendering.

This is the paragraph I most want to add. Your post claims append-only makes runs "resumable, auditable, and forkable" about pi sessions, then moves up to the org log and silently drops forkable. Yohei built exactly that — branch any run at any historical event, reconfigure, structurally diff against the parent, with replay caching so the shared prefix costs no new LLM calls — and calls it his most differentiated capability.

Admitting the gap is more credible than omitting it, and "the storage model gives us this for free and we haven't collected it" is a genuinely Simon-shaped paragraph. It also costs you nothing: the substrate is the hard part and you have it.

## 3. Positioning against ActiveGraph by name

The sharpest available contrast, and it's a difference in kind:

- He's SQLite-by-default, Postgres via an `EventStore` protocol, and the README explicitly says it is **not a production database**.
- Yours **is** the production store: multi-tenant, per-org scoped, with permissions compiled into the read path and a DB-level delete guard.

Also worth noting he's pure append with no supersession or tombstones, where you have both. Different tradeoff, not a worse one — pure append is simpler; supersession is what lets you correct a synced fact without rewriting history.

Naming a comparable is what gives a post an external hook, and it's what `shopifys-aquifer-in-the-open.mdx` already does well.

## What I'd skip

The three-beat opener (*"The graph is the world. Behaviors are physics. The trace is the proof."*) works in a README but is precisely the tricolon your BLOG_VOICE.md bans. And his blog voice generally — the self-improving-agents post is a 4,500-word citation-heavy survey with no first person, which would undo the Simon rewrite.

## Net effect

Adds roughly 250 words to a post currently at ~850 prose. Lands around 1,100, above your 600-700 guide target but the guide sets that for comparison posts, and this is a technical one.

Want me to write all three in? My recommendation is yes — 1 and 3 strengthen the argument, and 2 is the one that makes the post honest.

21	
22	Every row is an observation: a Slack thread a feed pulled, a payment webhook, a note an agent saved. 24	That was a convention for a long time, written in a `COMMENT ON TABLE` and in our AGENTS.md, which is to say it was enforced by nothing at all. Any psql session or admin tool could still wipe rows. So it became a trigger:

27	CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.events_block_direct_delete()
28	  RETURNS trigger AS $$
29	BEGIN
30	  IF pg_trigger_depth() > 1 THEN
31	    RETURN OLD; -- FK cascade (org delete) or another trigger's cleanup
32	  END IF;
33	  IF current_setting('lobu.allow_event_delete', true) = 'on' THEN
34	    RETURN OLD; -- sanctioned maintenance, transaction-scoped
35	  END IF;
36	  RAISE EXCEPTION
37	    'events is append-only: DELETE of event % blocked.',
38	    OLD.id

We are not the only ones landing here. Nakajima's [ActiveGraph](https://github.com/yoheinakajima/activegraph) is an event-sourced runtime for agents built on the same principle, where the working graph is a projection of the log and every mutation is an event. The interesting replays for us are not counterfactual runs but real consequences arriving late: the reply that came back, the payment that failed, the human who edited the arguments before approving.

That is also why we supersede instead of appending only. His model is simpler and I would pick it for a run-local trace. We need supersession because a fact we mirrored can change underneath us, and the honest record of that is a new observation pointing at the old one, not a rewritten row.

Two consistent traits worth noting: it's strictly **two-tone** (one red ink on warm off-white paper, no second color, no grey), and **tonal variation comes only from halftone dot density** — the prism image fades a beam by thinning dots, never by mixing a lighter red. Here's the prompt.

---

**Prompt for ChatGPT image generation:**

> A vintage technical illustration in a two-tone risograph style: a single bright red-orange ink (#E8342A) printed on warm off-white paper (#F5F1EA). No other colors, no grey, no gradients — all shading is done with visible halftone dot texture, coarse and slightly imperfect like mid-century offset printing. Subtle paper grain throughout.
>
> Subject: a long horizontal conveyor belt carrying a row of upright paper record cards, moving left to right, feeding into the open drawer of a large steel archive cabinet on the right. The cards are evenly spaced and identical in size, drawn in clean isometric perspective with crisp outlines.
>
> Key detail: beneath the belt, a second lower rail holds older duplicate cards, still present and neatly filed but rendered in a much lighter halftone — thinner dot density, faded but never erased. Thin lines connect a few of the faded lower cards up to their replacements on the main belt above, suggesting each new card supersedes an older one that is kept rather than discarded.
>
> Composition: 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, wide horizontal flow, generous negative space in the upper left, machinery weighted to the right. Flat editorial illustration, no text, no labels, no numbers, no lettering anywhere. Drawn with engraved line-work and stippling, like a 1960s industrial equipment catalogue.

---

Three things I deliberately built in:

**No text, stated three ways.** Image models put garbled lettering on filing cabinets and record cards by default, and it's the fastest way to look AI-generated. Your existing covers have zero text.

**Supersession as dot density, not opacity or color.** This is the one idea the cover needs to carry that a generic "archive" image wouldn't, and fading via thinner halftone is exactly how `d1-prism.webp` fades its beam. It stays inside the two-tone constraint.

**3:2 landscape with upper-left negative space.** All your covers are 1024×683-ish with the subject weighted to one side. If it comes out square it'll crop badly in the post header.

Two practical notes. ChatGPT will hand you a PNG, but every cover in `public/design/` is `.webp` at 130-230KB, so convert before committing — `cwebp -q 82 in.png -o public/design/prim-events.webp` gets you in range. And if the first result puts the faded cards somewhere confusing, the single most useful follow-up is *"keep the composition, make the lower faded row clearly the same cards as the upper row, just older"* — that relationship is the whole point and it's the part models tend to drop.

If it comes back too busy, cut the connecting lines from the prompt. The two-tier belt alone still reads as "new versions on top, old ones kept below."

content.text:
Confirmed in the schema: *"entity extraction all derive from here"*, and `entity_relationships` literally carries a `derivedFrom.sourceEventId` pointer. Entities are a second projection off the same log, alongside the current-events view. And the human loop is real too — those `entity_field_change` approvals I found earlier are humans approving proposed entity edits, which then land back as events.

So the picture has three parts, not one: **events accumulate → entities are built from them → a human approves changes → the decision returns as a new event.**

Here's the revised prompt.

---

**Prompt for ChatGPT image generation:**

> A vintage technical illustration in a two-tone risograph style: a single bright red-orange ink (#E8342A) printed on warm off-white paper (#F5F1EA). No other colors, no grey, no gradients — all shading is done with visible halftone dot texture, coarse and slightly imperfect like mid-century offset printing. Subtle paper grain throughout. Clean isometric perspective, engraved line-work and stippling, like a 1960s industrial equipment catalogue.
>
> A three-stage machine, flowing left to right, laid out as a loop.
>
> On the left, a long conveyor belt carries a row of evenly spaced upright paper record cards, all identical in size, feeding into the machine. This is the incoming stream.
>
> In the center, the belt feeds a sorting apparatus that assembles the flat cards into a small group of standing three-dimensional objects on a raised platform: a few simple filing-card boxes of different sizes, clearly constructed out of the incoming cards. Thin guide lines run from individual cards on the belt up to the objects they build, showing the objects are assembled from the stream rather than placed there.
>
> On the right, a single human figure in mid-century engraved style stands at a small inspection console beside the platform, seen in profile, examining one of the assembled objects held up in front of them. The figure has a lever or stamp in one hand.
>
> Closing the loop: a narrow return rail runs along the bottom of the frame from the human's console back to the start of the conveyor on the left, carrying a few stamped cards in the reverse direction, so the human's decisions rejoin the incoming stream. Draw a subtle arrowhead on this lower rail to show the reverse direction.
>
> Composition: 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, wide horizontal flow, generous negative space in the upper portion of the frame. No text, no labels, no numbers, no lettering anywhere.

---

What changed and why:

**Entities as assembled objects, not stored cards.** The center stage builds three-dimensional things *out of* the flat incoming cards, with guide lines showing which cards built what. That's the `derivedFrom.sourceEventId` relationship as a picture — entities are constructed from events, not filed alongside them.

**The human is inspecting, not operating.** Mid-loop, examining an assembled object with a stamp in hand. Approving proposed entity changes is exactly what your `entity_field_change` approvals are.

**The return rail is what makes it a loop.** The human's stamped decisions travel back to the start and rejoin the stream. That's your closing argument — approvals land as events, the next run reads them — and it's the one element the earlier prompt had no way to express.

I dropped the faded-superseded tier. Trying to show supersession *and* projection *and* the human loop in one frame will produce mush; supersession is the one the prose already handles well with the `NOT EXISTS` snippet.

One likely failure mode: models tend to draw the human large and centered, turning it into a portrait of a worker. If that happens, follow up with *"make the human figure smaller and keep the machine the main subject."* The machine should dominate.

Confidence: **high (95)** that events→entities is the correct architecture — verified in the table comment and the `derivedFrom` index, not assumed. **Medium (55)** on first-generation success; three stages plus a return rail is a lot to ask, and the return rail is the element most likely to get dropped or drawn as a second forward belt.

Two good questions, and they have opposite answers.

**Labels: no.** Not because labels are a bad idea, but because image models can't spell. Every cover in `public/design/` is text-free, and that's almost certainly deliberate for this reason — ChatGPT will render "EVENTS" as "EVNETS" or "EVENITS" on one of the three labels and you won't notice until it's live. Cover images also get shown small in the post header and in social cards, where 12px labels are illegible anyway.

If you want labels, the right move is to generate the image clean and add real text in a separate layer, where it's actual selectable type in your own font rather than a model's guess at letterforms. That's also how you'd get them to survive dark mode. I'd skip it — your other covers work without labels because the post's first paragraph does the explaining.

**The boxes as entities: partly, and my prompt was sloppy.** I wrote "filing-card boxes of different sizes," which is wrong twice over. Boxes read as *containers* — things you put cards into — which is exactly the storage metaphor the post argues against. And an entity isn't a container of events; it's a distinct object *derived* from them. A company entity isn't a box holding Slack messages.

The visual needs to say "assembled from" rather than "holds." Let me fix that stage of the prompt:

> In the center, the belt feeds a sorting apparatus that assembles the flat cards into a small group of standing three-dimensional forms on a raised platform: simple geometric solids of different shapes, a cube, a cylinder, a stepped block, each one visibly built up out of layered flat cards stacked and fused together, with the individual card edges still visible along their sides like sedimentary strata. Thin guide lines run from individual cards on the belt up to the forms they build.

"Layered cards fused into a solid, edges still visible like strata" is the accurate metaphor — the entity is a new object, but you can still see the events it was made of. That's `derivedFrom.sourceEventId` rendered honestly, and it kills the container reading.

Different shapes matter too: your entity types are heterogeneous (company, person, deal, goal), so identical forms would imply one type. Distinct solids say "different kinds of thing, same construction method."

One caveat: "sedimentary strata" is the phrase most likely to send the model somewhere geological. If the result looks like rock formations, swap it for *"like a stack of paper sheets glued into a solid block, cut edges visible."*

Everything else in the prompt stands.

Confidence: **high (90)** on the no-labels call — grounded in all eight existing covers being text-free plus known model spelling failure. **High (85)** that boxes were the wrong form; the container reading directly contradicts the post's thesis.

Yes, we can do the diagrams in the illustration style — that's the better answer, and I built the first one. But I need to be straight about what I verified.

**What's done.** `EntityProjectionDiagram.tsx` is written and rendering, wired into the post after the projection SQL with a short paragraph. It fills the real gap: entities being built from events, which the existing `TruthProxyDiagram` never showed and which the prose lost when we cut the entities section.

It borrows the illustration style from your own CSS rather than imitating it: halftone dot shading via `radial-gradient` (the same trick `landing.css` uses for `--lp-hair`), the `feTurbulence` paper grain from `--lp-grain`, and one accent ink. Your theme accent `#f5333a` and surface `#f3f1ea` are near-identical to the covers' `#E8342A` on `#F5F1EA`, so it wears the house style honestly while keeping real text, both themes, and `prefers-reduced-motion`.

Entities are drawn as solids with visible strata on the left edge — layers of events fused into one object, not boxes holding cards. That's the fix from your earlier question, and each shows "from N events" to make `derivedFrom.sourceEventId` legible. Stage 03 is the human: an agent proposes `deal.stage → closed_won`, approve/reject, and a return rail carrying the decision back as a new event.

**What I could not verify: I never saw it rendered.** Astro's preview server binds IPv6-only; Chrome resolves `localhost` to IPv4 and got connection-refused. I confirmed the split (`curl 127.0.0.1` → 000, `curl [::1]` → 200), but navigating Chrome to the IPv6 literal still failed, and I stopped rather than keep cycling. So I verified the diagram through the built HTML instead — all three stage labels, the entity names, "from 4/5/7 events", and the supersede line are present in `dist`. That proves it renders and the content is right. It does **not** prove it looks good. Spacing, the strata edge, and dark mode are unchecked.

Please open `http://[::1]:4400/blog/self-improving-agents-are-event-sourced/` in your own browser and look. That's the one thing outstanding.

**On generating more images:** I'd still keep generated art for the cover only. In-body, these HTML diagrams beat illustrations on text crispness and dark mode, and now they carry the same visual language. Your cover is the genuine gap — `prim-channels` is a broadcast tower, which contradicts the post.

Confidence: **high (90)** that the content and structure are correct — verified in built HTML. **Low (30)** on visual polish — unviewed, and that's exactly the "never report done off a green build" case your AGENTS.md calls out.

There's a real `notifications/service` and agents can send via a `notify` tool. That's enough to write the section accurately.

Here's what I verified, and one correction to your framing before the prompts.

**Interaction types are real, but there are three, not many.** The DB constraint allows `none`, `approval`, `suggestion`. I found `question` and `link_button` in TypeScript, but only in test files — they're not in the check constraint, so I won't claim them as shipped. The envelope on an approval event carries a JSON schema for the proposed input, which is what makes the card an editable form rather than a yes/no button. That's the "events build UI" idea and it's genuinely true.

**One claim I could not verify: every MCP tool call being an event.** I grepped for MCP calls writing events and found nothing. What exists is *attribution* — the screenshot showed "Requested by mcp_client_…" on an approval event. So gated actions from an MCP client are logged with their origin; ordinary reads aren't. Your memory notes already flag this distinction (`mcp_binding_is_attribution_not_authz`). I'd write the narrower true version.

---

Now the prompts. The fix for ambiguity is a **fixed visual vocabulary** reused across all three, so a reader learns the shapes once.

**The vocabulary (paste this at the top of every prompt):**

> Style: vintage two-tone risograph technical illustration. A single bright red-orange ink (#E8342A) on warm off-white paper (#F5F1EA). No other colors, no grey. All shading is visible halftone dot texture — density is the only tonal control, denser reads darker. Subtle paper grain. Clean isometric perspective, engraved line-work and stippling, like a 1960s industrial equipment catalogue. No text, no labels, no numbers, no lettering anywhere.
>
> Consistent objects across this set: a FLAT RECTANGULAR CARD is an event. A SOLID CUBE built from stacked, visibly layered cards (cut edges showing like a glued paper block) is an entity. A SHEET HELD IN A CLAMP OR UNDER A STAMP is a pending approval. A HUMAN FIGURE in profile is the reviewer.

**Image 1 — the cover (events → entities → human → back):**

> [vocabulary] A three-stage machine flowing left to right. Left: a conveyor belt carrying evenly spaced flat cards. Center: a press that stacks the flat cards into three solid cubes of different sizes on a raised platform, the layered card edges clearly visible along each cube's side, with thin guide lines from individual cards to the cube they built. 56:## Driving the paired Owletto extension (connector debugging)
57-
58:The cookie-forging above and `claude-in-chrome` both drive a *separate* browser that lacks the user's real logged-in sessions — Revolut, for instance, redirects them to `sso.revolut.com/signin`. To run JS or browser actions in the **paired Owletto extension** (the Chrome that holds the user's live sessions, which is what extension-scrape connectors like Revolut/LinkedIn use), go through the connector-operations bridge instead. No deploy required.
59-
60-`lobu connector run` is the wrong tool here — it only does local Playwright/CDP against a `browser_session` auth profile, so it errors `Missing --auth-profile` for device-worker connectors (Revolut has no auth profile).
61-
62-For one-off actions, the `lobu call` CLI is the quickest path (usually org `buremba`; connection id from `lobu call manage_connections --org buremba --arg action=list --raw`):
63-
64-```bash
65-lobu call manage_operations --org buremba --arg action=execute \
66-  --arg connection_id=<chrome-connection-id> --arg operation_key=navigate \
67-  --arg input:='{"url":"https://app.slack.com/...","wait_for_load":true,"open_in_new_tab":true}' --raw
68-```
69-
70-For multi-step scripts, use the SDK `operations` namespace via `lobu memory exec` / `run_sdk`:
71-
72-```js
73-// chrome connection id: client.connections.list() → connector_key 'chrome'
74-const ops = await client.operations.listAvailable({ connection_id: CHROME_CONN_ID });
75-// navigate opens a fresh background tab in the paired Chrome and returns tab_id
76-const nav = await client.operations.execute({
77-  connection_id: CHROME_CONN_ID, operation_key: 'navigate',
78-  input: { url: 'https://app.revolut.com/transactions', open_in_new_tab: true, wait_for_load: true },
79-});
80-// evaluate runs arbitrary JS on that tab and returns the JSON-serialised result
81-await client.operations.execute({
82-  connection_id: CHROME_CONN_ID, operation_key: 'evaluate',
83-  input: { tab_id: nav.output.tab_id, expression: '(async()=>{ /* read DOM */ return out })()', await_promise: true },
--
93:- **Connector-side changes ship via re-apply, not the app release.** Per-org connectors (`examples/personal-agent`) live in `connector_definitions`/`connector_versions` and only update on `lobu apply` (or `connections.installConnector` for a single bundle). An app deploy that adds a *capability* (e.g. `show_notification`) does nothing until the connector that *calls* it is re-applied. **And a new chrome action also needs the matching handler in the extension build** — dispatching `show_notification` to an older installed extension fails with `Owletto for Chrome: unknown dispatch ... action_key='show_notification'`. So three things gate such a notification: an up-to-date extension build (the handler), a re-applied connector (the call), and macOS notification permission on the extension.

content.text: Now the interaction-types section, using the envelope image and the three verified types.

input.old_string: Two consequences I'd flag.
input.new_string:
What makes that card an actual interface is the envelope on the event. Alongside the proposed input, the event carries the JSON schema describing that input. The web app feeds the schema into a form, so the reviewer can edit the arguments before approving rather than voting yes or no on someone else's draft. The same event renders as a Slack card with buttons, and both paths call the same tool underneath. The UI is a function of the event, which is why a new interaction type doesn't need a new screen.

![The interaction envelope: the event underneath, and the schema that defines which fields the reviewer can edit](/blog/interaction-envelope.webp)

There are three interaction types today, and the constraint on the table is the honest list: `none` for the overwhelming majority, `approval` for a gated write, and `suggestion` for something the agent offers without blocking on it. That's a smaller vocabulary than I expected we'd need.

Two consequences I'd flag.

input.new_string:
None of that is clever, which is the part I'd defend. The model in the loop gets better a few times a year, when a lab ships something. The agent gets better every week, because the substrate underneath it remembers. I'd rather own the second one.

## Notifications are a query, not a firehose

The last piece falls out of the same shape. Once every consequential thing is an event with an envelope, notifying a human is a selection over the log rather than a separate delivery system. An agent calls `notify`, the recipients resolve to members, and the notification is itself recorded, so what got surfaced to whom is as inspectable as everything else.

This is the part I'd be careful with, and I mean careful in the product sense rather than the engineering sense. A system that knows what you approved, what you ignored until it expired, and what you edited before letting through has everything it needs to get very good at pulling your attention. The same feedback that makes the agent more useful makes it better at interrupting you. Optimizing engagement on that substrate would work, which is exactly why it's the wrong objective to point it at.

The one guardrail I'll defend is the one already in the approvals path: expired is a distinct status from rejected, and nothing escalates on silence. An agent should learn from the decisions you actually made, not from how many times it managed to make you look.

content.text: This is the ETL analogy image, and it's very good — full pipeline with the decision loop feeding back as new OLTP events. Let me check the other two.

This is the Lobu-side counterpart of the same structure: EVENT LOG → BEHAVIOR RUN → SHAPED DATA → INTERFACES (activity, approvals, briefs, forms), with interactions returning as NEW EVENTS. This pairs with the OLTP one perfectly.

Now to your actual question, because it has a real answer and it isn't quite the one the images imply.

**No, that's not medallion architecture.** Medallion is Databricks' bronze/silver/gold: raw → cleaned/conformed → business-level aggregates, three *persisted* tables, each a materialized copy of the last. Your pipeline is closer to **Kappa architecture** — one immutable log as the system of record, with everything downstream derived from it. Jay Kreps' 2014 argument, and the same lineage as Kafka log compaction.

The distinctions that matter:

**Bronze is a landing zone. Your log is the source of truth.** In medallion, bronze is where raw data lands before being cleaned; gold is what people query. In yours, the log is what everything reads *through* — the `NOT EXISTS` view means current state is a query over the log, not a copy of it.

**Medallion tiers are materialized. Yours are projections.** Bronze/silver/gold are three physical tables you maintain and reconcile. Your entities are derived with `derivedFrom.sourceEventId` pointing back, so the derivation is traceable rather than a rebuild step.

**Medallion has no human in the loop.** That's the piece your images capture that no warehouse pattern has. In the medallion world an analyst reads gold and writes a doc; the decision leaves the system. In yours the approval is an event that supersedes the proposal, so the decision re-enters the substrate. That loop-back rail is the actual differentiator, and it's why the OLTP/CDC image is a useful *contrast* rather than a match.

Where the ETL analogy does hold: CDC ≈ your connectors, warehouse tables ≈ your entities, dashboards ≈ your interfaces. That's a good on-ramp for a data-engineering reader. Where it breaks: warehouses are read-only endpoints, and the decision loop is where you diverge.

If you want this in the post, the honest framing is "this looks like CDC into a warehouse, and the analogy holds until the decision comes back."

**On the images:** `last1` and `last2` are both excellent and near-identical in structure — `last2` (with APPROVALS/BRIEFS/FORMS as separate interface types) is the stronger one and would slot straight into the interaction-types section. `last3` is the OLTP contrast piece. All three have correct spelling and legible labels.

I haven't installed any of them yet. Currently in the post: `prim-events.webp` (cover) and `interaction-envelope.webp`.

Confidence: **high (90)** on the Kappa-vs-medallion distinction; that's a well-established architectural split, and the projection-not-materialization difference is verified in your schema. **High (95)** on the image contents — I viewed all six.

Next actions:
- Tell me which to install: I'd take `last2` for the interactions section, and optionally `last3` if you want the ETL contrast paragraph written.
- Want the "this is Kappa, not medallion" framing as a short section? It's a good hook for data-engineering readers and I can source it to Kreps.
- Still unviewed by me: the rendered post (IPv6 preview issue).
- Commit when settled: post + 2 diagram components + webp files, by explicit path.
which one do you think is better?

Depends which slot, so let me split it.

**For the cover: `last1`, and I'd switch from what's currently installed.**

`prim-events.webp` (the one I installed) says events → entities → reviewer → back. True, but it's the narrow story.

`last1` says events → behavior run → shaped data → template → interface, with three different people seeing the same data rendered differently, and the return rail underneath. That's a bigger claim and it's the one your post actually makes now that the interaction-envelope and notification sections are in. The caption "interfaces render the same data differently for different people" is the post's thesis in one line.

One real drawback: `last1` is the most text-heavy of the six, with five headers plus six caption blocks. At cover size in a post header or social card, none of that will be readable — it'll read as texture. That's survivable for a cover (the current `prim-channels` is decorative too) but it's a genuine cost. `prim-events` is cleaner at small sizes.

If you want the cover to work at thumbnail scale, keep `prim-events`. If you want the cover to carry the argument for someone who stops to look, `last1`.

**For the body: `last2`, definitely.**

It's `last1`'s structure but with the interface types called out — ACTIVITY, APPROVALS, BRIEFS, FORMS — which is exactly the section I just wrote about interaction types building UI. And its bottom rail is captioned "interactions in the interfaces create new events that re-enter the event log," which is the loop the closing section argues. It's the single most on-message image of the six.

**`last3` I'd skip** unless you want the Kappa-vs-medallion framing written. On its own, an OLTP/CDC/warehouse diagram in a post about agent memory invites the reader to think you're describing a warehouse, which is the misreading I'd rather avoid. It only earns its place next to a paragraph explaining where the analogy breaks.

So my recommendation: **`last2` in the body** (clear win), and **`last1` as cover only if you accept it's decorative at small sizes**.

Want me to install `last2` in the interactions section — replacing or alongside `interaction-envelope.webp`? The envelope image is more specific about the schema-defines-the-form mechanism; `last2` is better at the overall shape. They're not redundant, but two illustrations plus an HTML diagram in one section is a lot.
should we do a seperate blog post about this ETL for autonomous agents?

Yes — and I think it's a better post than the section would be.

**The case for splitting it.** The current post's thesis is "self-improvement is a storage problem." The ETL post's thesis is different: "agent platforms are rebuilding the data stack, and here's which parts transfer and which don't." Those are two arguments. Bolting the second onto the first would blur the first, and the current post is already at ~1,300 words with two SQL blocks, two HTML diagrams, and an illustration.

It also has a real audience hook the current post doesn't. Data engineers have spent a decade on CDC, medallion, dbt, and lineage. Telling them "your agent memory layer is a warehouse with a decision loop" gives them a way in, and that's a different reader than the one who clicks a post about event sourcing.

**The strongest version of the argument** is where the analogy *breaks*, not where it holds. The mapping is easy — CDC ≈ connectors, fact tables ≈ entities, dashboards ≈ interfaces. Three real differences:

The warehouse is a dead end; the decision leaves the system. An analyst reads gold, writes a doc, and whatever happens next is invisible to the pipeline. In yours the approval supersedes the proposal and re-enters the log, so the loop closes. That's `last3` versus `last2` as a visual pairing, and it's why those two images are worth having.

Medallion materializes; you project. Bronze/silver/gold are three physical copies you reconcile. Your entities carry `derivedFrom.sourceEventId` and current state is a `NOT EXISTS` view. That's Kappa, not medallion, and the distinction is load-bearing rather than pedantic.

Warehouses have no permission problem at read time. dbt models don't ask who's asking. Yours compiles org scope, connection visibility, and resource membership into every read, because an agent answering for one person must not surface another's Gmail.

**The honest risk:** it's an analogy post, which is the easiest kind to write badly. If it's just "X is like Y" for 800 words it's forgettable. It works only if you commit to the three breakages and name the tradeoffs — including that a warehouse beats you on analytical query performance and on decades of tooling.

**What I'd need before writing it.** I'd want to verify the entity-derivation path more carefully than I have. I've confirmed the `derivedFrom.sourceEventId` index and the events table comment, but I haven't traced how entities are actually built from events, and an ETL-framed post lives or dies on that being described accurately. That's a bounded piece of reading.

My recommendation: yes, write it, but **after** you commit the current post. That one is finished modulo the cover choice and has been sitting uncommitted across two sessions, and starting a second post before landing the first is how both stay unfinished. Per your one-branch-one-concern rule it's a separate branch anyway.

Confidence: **high (85)** that it's a genuinely distinct post rather than a section — the theses don't overlap. **Medium (60)** on the three-breakages structure being the right shape; that's my read, not something I've tested against how the argument lands.

Next actions:
- Land the current post first: pick the cover (`prim-events` vs `last1`), install `last2` in the body if you want it, then commit and PR.
- Then I trace the entity-derivation path and draft the ETL post on a fresh branch.
- Open question for that post: do you want it aimed at data engineers (lean hard on dbt/medallion/Kappa vocabulary) or at agent builders (use the data stack as the familiar thing)? Different posts.
or data-warehouse for autonomous agents?

"Data warehouse" is the better noun, but I'd push back on it slightly, because it undersells what you built.

**Why it beats ETL.** ETL names a *process* — the moving of data. Your interesting claim isn't about movement, it's about the store: what's kept, who can read it, what's derived from it. A post called "ETL for Agents" promises a pipeline discussion and then spends most of its time on storage semantics. "Data warehouse" names the thing.

It's also the more provocative title, and provocative is what gets a post read. "ETL for agents" sounds like plumbing. "The Data Warehouse for Autonomous Agents" sounds like a claim about what layer of the stack this is.

**Where it undersells you.** A warehouse is read-optimized and terminal. Data goes in, analysts query, decisions leave. Yours writes back — the approval supersedes the proposal, the action's outcome lands as another event. If the title says warehouse and the post's best argument is "except it closes the loop," you've named yourself after the thing you're differentiating from.

Two ways to handle that, and I'd pick the second:

**Lean in and subvert it.** "The Data Warehouse for Autonomous Agents" as the title, then open by conceding the frame is wrong in one specific way and spend the post on that. Classic structure, works well, and the borrowed familiarity does the audience-acquisition work.

**Name the gap instead.** Something like "Agents Need a Warehouse That Writes Back." Less familiar, but it's the actual thesis, and it doesn't need a paragraph of walking-back.

I'd go with the first. Your existing titles ("The Context Layer Is an Event Store", "The Agent Loop Is the New SaaS") are all declarative claims-with-a-familiar-noun, so it matches the house pattern, and the subversion is exactly what makes the post worth writing.

One thing to check: you already have `the-context-layer-is-an-event-store.mdx`. There's real overlap risk — that post presumably argues the context layer is a log, and this one would argue it's a warehouse-that-writes-back. Worth me reading it before drafting, so the new post engages it rather than repeating it.

Also worth noting: "warehouse" invites the medallion comparison directly, which is good, since the Kappa-not-medallion distinction is one of your three strongest points.

Confidence: **high (80)** that "data warehouse" is the better frame than ETL. **Medium (55)** on the exact title — that's taste, and you know your audience better than I do.

Next actions:
- Land the current post first (cover choice, then commit) — still my recommendation before starting a second.
- When you're ready, I read `the-context-layer-is-an-event-store.mdx` first to find the seam between the two posts.

11	Tasman Analytics published [How to build a context layer](https://www.tasman.ai/news/how-to-build-a-context-layer), the best writeup yet of a failure everyone running data agents has seen. The semantic layer is the governed what. Nobody wrote down the governed why. So the agent computes churn correctly, sees a spike in March, and invents an explanation, because the billing migration that wrote 1,900 fake cancellations was never stored anywhere a machine can read.
12	
13	The numbers behind this are brutal. Anthropic found the same model went from at most 21% correct to over 95% on their internal analytics once it had the right skills around it: procedural routing, reference files, a governed data foundation. Then accuracy fell back toward 65% within a month as the underlying models drifted and nobody kept the skill docs current. In that system the limiting variable was the context, not the model.
14	
15	Tasman's conclusion is that no product can solve this, because the content does not exist yet. It lives in analysts' heads and scrolled Slack threads. I agree that it is a workflow problem. I think the governed *why* wants one substrate, not four.
16	
17	## The governed why wants one substrate
18	
19	Their design spreads the why across four homes: column caveats in dbt YAML, a business_events table in the warehouse, decision records as markdown in git, and verified queries pinned in the semantic layer. Four systems, four maintenance rituals, glued together by three MCP servers and the model's context window.
20	
21	I don't think all four collapse into one product, and I want to be honest about which parts don't. A dbt caveat belongs next to the model so the code and the caveat change in the same commit. A verified query belongs where routing uses it. Those have a source of truth and it isn't Lobu. But they can be *mirrored* into one queryable place through connectors, the way you'd sync any source, so an agent reads one store instead of stitching three MCP servers together at answer time. Mirroring is not the same as owning. The authoritative copy stays where the authoring workflow lives.
22	
23	What genuinely does want to live in one store is the part nobody owns today: the dated business events, the definition changelog, and the decisions. We took Tasman's fictional company, Kelder Coffee, and built that overlay on Lobu without changing a line of Lobu. A `business-event` entity type holds the migration, the definition change, the courier strike, each with affected metrics and a link to the incident. The changelog is not a table anyone maintains. Events in Lobu are append-only and versioned by supersession, so saving churn v2 with a pointer to v1 *is* the changelog. Query the current definition or the full history, same store.
24	
25	The live series is never materialized. A read-only connector runs the churn rollup live against the customer's own Postgres, and a sandboxed script joins that series with the business events and the definition versions in plain JavaScript. The context doesn't just annotate the numbers, it *drives the query*. March reads raw 550, and the billing-migration event carries a structured adjustment, so the script subtracts the ~500 artifact rows and reports 50 — the real cancellations that month still stand, the month isn't thrown away. The churn definition's v2 (a dunning-grace exclusion) is a `WHERE` fragment the script applies per month, so a month after the v2 boundary is counted at 38 where v1 would have said 50 — same warehouse, different number, because the definition changed the query and not just the label. Every deviation cites its source. No model in the loop.
26	
27	That is a deterministic composition, and it proves seeded context can be composed into a sourced answer. It does not yet prove an agent *retrieves* the right context and writes the right query on its own — the repo ships that eval, WITH-context versus baseline, and it passes as a deterministic proxy; the live-agent run just needs a model key wired in. I'm calling that out rather than dressing the proxy up as the real thing.
28	
29	The trust loop is a pinned verified query: store the approved answer, re-run the SQL later, diff the rows. When the warehouse moves under a definition, the rows change and the diff fires before someone repeats a stale number in a board deck. It is a result-drift canary, not a measure of whether an agent stayed accurate. Those are different failures and the honest version says so.
30	
31	The runnable example is in the repo (link goes live when the PRs below land).
32	
33	## Capture is an ingestion problem, not a documentation problem
34	
35	"The content does not exist yet" is the strongest line in their piece, and their fix is PR templates and incident runbooks. Asking humans to write documentation is how we got here.
36	
37	The why gets spoken exactly once, in a Slack thread, at the moment the CFO agrees to exclude returns from revenue. Lobu's watchers already sit in those threads. Capturing that sentence as a decision event, typed, dated, linked back to the thread, is ingestion. The human approves it instead of authoring it. That is the difference between a context layer that fills up and a wiki that rots.
38	
39	## Context has to be pushed, not searched
40	
41	An agent that doesn't know March is poisoned has no reason to search for "is March poisoned." The jump from 21 to 95 comes from context sitting in the prompt before the first query gets written, not from a retrieval the agent thinks to run.
42	
43	This one we had to fix in our own house. Entity-type and field descriptions were stored in Lobu and never rendered into the instructions agents receive, so we render them now, and we added a `guidance` event kind: org-level context that admins author and every agent sees on every request. The data model is just an event, which is the nice part, editing guidance means superseding it and the history of your own operating instructions is more memory. But storing it is the easy half. Rendering it, gating who can author it, capping how much lands in the prompt, and injecting it safely is the actual work, and that was a real branch, not a config flag. A prompt budget also means this can't hold arbitrary org context, so selective retrieval doesn't go away, it sits underneath.
44	
45	One more thing nobody in this conversation mentions: access control. The moment real decisions go into a shared layer, "who may see this why" is the first question an enterprise asks. Lobu compiles per-connection and per-resource visibility straight into the query SQL, so a private connection's data or a repo you're not a member of never surfaces in a coworker's answer. Arbitrary per-decision authorization is further out, but having the fence compiled into the read path rather than bolted on afterward is the part that's genuinely hard to retrofit.
46	
47	What's honestly still missing is more than plumbing. Warehouse connectors in cloud needed real egress hardening before we could open them, and that landed. Lineage from a dbt manifest needs an SPI addition. Federated metric definitions from Cube or Snowflake are designed and not wired, and reflecting them means the metric compiler can't assume Postgres dialect. Beyond our own code: the Slack-to-decision capture I described is the design, not a shipped demo, and the harder-than-storage question of whether a captured sentence is actually an authoritative, correctly-scoped decision is editorial judgment a human still makes. And the agent eval passes as a deterministic proxy today; the live-agent version, an actual model answering the March question with the context pushed versus without, needs a provider key wired in and is the honest remaining gap. So the honest claim is narrow: the governed why is a small, versioned, access-controlled event store, and it mirrors the semantic layer and the warehouse rather than replacing them. That is a component, not a fifth product you buy, and you can run it today.
48	
49	*Also worth reading: Tasman's [semantic vs. context essay](https://www.tasman.ai/news/we-are-still-confusing-the-semantic-layer-for-context-its-not), Yali Sassoon on [why a semantic layer is not a context layer](https://datacreation.substack.com/p/a-semantic-layer-is-not-a-context), and Snowflake's [agent context layer](https://www.snowflake.com/en/blog/agent-context-layer-trustworthy-data-agents/).*

Having read it: **new post, definitely.** Not a close call.

That post is already doing something specific and doing it well. It's a *response* to Tasman, structured around their four-homes design, and its thesis is "the governed why wants one substrate." It's tagged `analytics`, it argues mirroring-not-owning, and it ends on an unusually honest list of what's missing. Reworking it into a warehouse post would wreck a piece that's already coherent — and it's published, dated 2026-07-12, so editing it rewrites the record rather than adding to it.

More importantly, the overlap is smaller than I assumed. That post is about the *why* layer: decisions, definition changelogs, business events annotating metrics. Yours would be about the **store's shape** — projections vs. materialization, permissions in the read path, the write-back loop. Different arguments that happen to share a substrate.

There's also a genuine seam to write against, which is the best possible setup. That post says Lobu "mirrors the semantic layer and the warehouse rather than replacing them" and calls itself "a component, not a fifth product you buy." The warehouse post picks that up: if it mirrors a warehouse, why isn't it just a warehouse? Answer: because warehouses are terminal and this one writes back. You can link to the earlier post as the setup rather than repeating it.

One thing that changes my earlier advice, though. That post already deploys warehouse vocabulary heavily — semantic layer, dbt, metric compiler, Cube/Snowflake, lineage. So the data-engineering audience is *already* addressed. The new post shouldn't re-explain medallion to them. The sharper angle is the one the existing post explicitly defers: it says "arbitrary per-decision authorization is further out" and treats access control as one paragraph. In a warehouse-framed post, permissions-compiled-into-the-read-path is a headline difference from every warehouse ever built, not a footnote.

So I'd aim the new post at **agent builders**, using the warehouse as the familiar anchor, and let the existing post keep the data-engineering readership.

Three-way split, roughly: the event-sourcing post is "the storage is a log." The context-layer post is "the governed why belongs in that log." The warehouse post is "this shaped store is what agents need instead of a warehouse, and here's what it does that a warehouse can't."

One correction to something I said earlier: I suggested `last3` (the OLTP/CDC image) risked implying you're describing a warehouse. In a post *titled* around the warehouse comparison, that image stops being a liability and becomes the setup — pair it with `last2` and the contrast does the work visually.

Confidence: **high (90)** that it should be new — the existing post is a published response piece with a different thesis. **Medium (65)** on the agent-builder framing being right; that's a judgment about audience allocation, and you know your readers better.

- Land the current post: pick the cover (`prim-events` vs `last1`), decide on `last2` in the body, then commit and PR.
- Then a fresh branch for the warehouse post; I'd start by tracing the actual entity-derivation path so the projection claims are verified rather than inferred.
