---
title: "The Data Warehouse for Autonomous Agents"
description: "Agent memory looks like a warehouse: connectors are CDC, entities are the modelled tables, the app is the BI layer. The analogy holds until the decision comes back, and that is the part worth building."
date: 2026-07-29
author: Burak Emre Kabakcı
authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba
tags: [architecture, agents, memory, analytics]
cover: /design/prim-memory.webp
draft: false
---

Every team building agent memory ends up rebuilding the data stack, usually without noticing. You start with "the agent should remember things," you add a sync from Slack, then one from your CRM, then you need the same person from both to be one person, then someone asks why the agent said 40 and the dashboard says 38. That is not a novel AI problem. That is a warehouse, and data engineering spent fifteen years on it.

So it is worth taking the analogy seriously, because most of it transfers. Connectors are change data capture. The append-only log is your raw landing zone. Entities are the modelled tables. The app is the BI layer on top. If you have built a warehouse you already know how most of an agent memory layer should be shaped, and you should reuse that instinct rather than inventing vocabulary.

![The classic pipeline: OLTP systems, change capture, warehouse tables, analysts, executives](/blog/warehouse-pipeline.webp)

Then the analogy breaks, in three specific places. The breakages are the interesting part.

## A warehouse is terminal. This one writes back.

Look at the pipeline above and follow it to the end. An analyst reads the dashboard, writes a brief, and an executive decides something. Whatever happens next leaves the system. The decision might land in Slack, or a board deck, or nowhere. The warehouse has no idea it happened, and next quarter's model has no way to learn that the March number was thrown out for a reason.

That terminal shape is fine when the output is a human reading a chart. It is useless when the output is an agent that acts, because the whole point is that the next run should know what the last decision was.

![The same shape for agents: the log, the run, shaped data, and the interfaces that write back](/blog/agent-warehouse.webp)

So the loop closes. When an agent wants to do something consequential, one transaction writes a pending run and a pending approval event. The human's decision is not an update to that event; it appends a new one pointing at it, stamped with who decided. The action's outcome supersedes again later, carrying the output or the error. The approval, the rejection, the arguments a reviewer edited before letting it through: all of it is in the same store the agent reads from tomorrow.

That is the difference between a system that reports and a system that improves. I wrote about the storage mechanics of that loop in [Self-Improving Agents Are Event-Sourced](/blog/self-improving-agents-are-event-sourced/).

## Medallion materializes. This projects.

The instinct from warehouse-land is medallion: bronze for raw, silver for cleaned, gold for business-level aggregates. Three tiers, each a physical table you maintain, each a copy of the one before it.

We went the other way, and it is closer to what Jay Kreps called [kappa architecture](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/questioning-the-lambda-architecture/): one immutable log, everything else derived from it. Current state is not a tier. It is a view whose entire mechanism is one `NOT EXISTS` over the supersession pointer, so a row is current exactly when nothing supersedes it.

The entity tables that do get materialized are explicitly demoted. The comment on ours says it plainly:

> Trigger-maintained projection of the latest entity_field event per (entity_id, field). Rebuildable cache; the events log is the source of truth.

A rebuildable cache, not a tier. That distinction sounds academic until you have to correct something. In a medallion stack, fixing a bad silver row means a backfill and a reconciliation, and the question "what did gold say last Tuesday" often has no answer. Here the correction is an append that points at what it replaced, and the old value is still there. You are trading storage for the ability to answer questions about your own past, which is a trade agents make worth it, because an agent's mistakes need to be explainable after the fact.

## Warehouses do not ask who is asking. This one has to.

This is the difference that surprised me most, and the one I would push hardest on if you are building this.

A dbt model does not care who runs it. Row-level security exists in warehouses, and plenty of teams use it, but it is bolted to the edges: a view here, a masking policy there, mostly enforced by which dashboard someone can open. That is survivable when the consumer is a human with a login and a job title.

It is not survivable when the consumer is an agent answering on behalf of whoever asked. The same agent serves everyone in the org. If permissions live in the UI, then one badly-worded question is all it takes for a coworker's Gmail to end up in an answer, and nobody finds out.

So visibility is compiled into the read path rather than applied after it. Every read carries a scope, and org scoping, per-connection visibility, and per-resource membership all become part of the SQL that runs. A connection backed by a personal OAuth login is forced private by a database trigger. When a membership sync goes stale the gate fails closed, so a stalled sync hides data instead of leaking it.

The warehouse world has an answer to this and it is called governance, and it is usually a layer you buy. In an agent store it cannot be a layer, because there is no seam between "query" and "answer" for it to sit in.

## What the warehouse still does better

I do not want to oversell the comparison. If your question is analytical, a warehouse wins and it is not close. Columnar storage, decades of query optimization, and a dbt ecosystem that is genuinely excellent all beat a Postgres event log for scanning a billion rows to get one aggregate. We do not try to compete there. Metrics that need the warehouse read the warehouse, live, over a connector, and the answer is composed rather than copied.

The claim is narrower than "replace your warehouse." It is that the store an agent reads and writes has a different shape than the store an analyst queries: it closes the loop, it projects instead of materializing, and it carries permissions into the read path. Those three requirements do not come from AI. They come from the consumer being autonomous, and from the consumer acting on what it finds.

The truth stays in the systems that own it. What this store keeps is what was observed, who may see it, and what every agent did about it.

Start with the [docs](/getting-started/), or read how the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/) works.

content.text:
Yes, worth explaining — but the honest mapping is **not** Snowflake, and I'd push back on that specific comparison.

**What the schema says.** A Behavior is *"per-agent scheduled jobs with a cron-style cadence. Each tick enqueues a runs row."* The Behavior table is the schedule definition; the `runs` row is the unit of execution, with `status transitions pending → claimed → running → completed | failed | timeout via heartbeat-based reaping`.

That's a scheduled job producing a claimable work item. Snowflake's engine is a columnar MPP query executor — massively parallel scan-and-aggregate over immutable micro-partitions. Nothing about a Behavior resembles that. If you map Behavior → Snowflake, the first data engineer who reads it will say "no, that's a task queue," and they'll be right.

**The accurate mappings, in order of how well they hold:**

**Behavior ≈ dbt model on a schedule, or Snowflake Task.** Snowflake *Tasks* (not Snowflake the engine) are the real analogue: scheduled units that run on a cadence, can chain, and are defined declaratively. A Behavior is a scheduled run against the log that writes derived events back. That's genuinely close, and it's the comparison I'd make.

**`runs` ≈ the orchestrator, not the warehouse.** Pending → claimed → running with heartbeat reaping is Airflow/Dagster task-instance semantics. A warehouse has no equivalent because a warehouse doesn't own execution.

**Where it breaks, and this is the good part.** A dbt model is a pure function: SQL in, table out, deterministic, idempotent. A Behavior invokes a model and can take actions with side effects in systems you don't own. You cannot re-run it to get the same answer, and you cannot re-run it *safely*. That's why approvals exist, and why `runs` has a claim protocol — a dbt model never needs one because re-running is free.

That breakage is a genuinely strong addition to the warehouse post. It gives you a fourth difference alongside the three you have: **the transform isn't idempotent, so orchestration semantics have to be stricter than a warehouse's.**

**One caution.** Your AGENTS.md says "Behavior" is the agent-facing name and `watcher` is internal DB vocabulary that must not leak into public surfaces. Blog posts aren't in the enforced list, but I'd keep the post on "Behavior" and avoid quoting the `watchers` table comment verbatim.

So: yes to explaining Behaviors, no to Snowflake-the-engine, yes to Snowflake Tasks / dbt-on-a-schedule with the idempotency breakage as the punchline.

Confidence: **high (90)** on the mapping being scheduled-job rather than query-engine — read directly from the table comments. **High (85)** that the non-idempotency point is the strongest version of this addition.

28	So the loop closes. When an agent wants to do something consequential, one transaction writes a pending run and a pending approval event. The human's decision is not an update to that event; it appends a new one pointing at it, stamped with who decided. The action's outcome supersedes again later, carrying the output or the error. The approval, the rejection, the arguments a reviewer edited before letting it through: all of it is in the same store the agent reads from tomorrow.
29	
30	That is the difference between a system that reports and a system that improves. I wrote about the storage mechanics of that loop in [Self-Improving Agents Are Event-Sourced](/blog/self-improving-agents-are-event-sourced/).
31	
32	## Medallion materializes. This projects.
33	
34	The instinct from warehouse-land is medallion: bronze for raw, silver for cleaned, gold for business-level aggregates. Three tiers, each a physical table you maintain, each a copy of the one before it.
35	
36	We went the other way, and it is closer to what Jay Kreps called [kappa architecture](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/questioning-the-lambda-architecture/): one immutable log, everything else derived from it. Current state is not a tier. It is a view whose entire mechanism is one `NOT EXISTS` over the supersession pointer, so a row is current exactly when nothing supersedes it.
37	
38	The entity tables that do get materialized are explicitly demoted. The comment on ours says it plainly:
39	
40	> Trigger-maintained projection of the latest entity_field event per (entity_id, field). Rebuildable cache; the events log is the source of truth.
41	
42	A rebuildable cache, not a tier. That distinction sounds academic until you have to correct something. In a medallion stack, fixing a bad silver row means a backfill and a reconciliation, and the question "what did gold say last Tuesday" often has no answer. Here the correction is an append that points at what it replaced, and the old value is still there. You are trading storage for the ability to answer questions about your own past, which is a trade agents make worth it, because an agent's mistakes need to be explainable after the fact.
43	
44	## Warehouses do not ask who is asking. This one has to.
45	
46	This is the difference that surprised me most, and the one I would push hardest on if you are building this.
47	
48	A dbt model does not care who runs it. Row-level security exists in warehouses, and plenty of teams use it, but it is bolted to the edges: a view here, a masking policy there, mostly enforced by which dashboard someone can open. That is survivable when the consumer is a human with a login and a job title.
49	
50	It is not survivable when the consumer is an agent answering on behalf of whoever asked. The same agent serves everyone in the org. If permissions live in the UI, then one badly-worded question is all it takes for a coworker's Gmail to end up in an answer, and nobody finds out.
51	
52	So visibility is compiled into the read path rather than applied after it. Every read carries a scope, and org scoping, per-connection visibility, and per-resource membership all become part of the SQL that runs. A connection backed by a personal OAuth login is forced private by a database trigger. When a membership sync goes stale the gate fails closed, so a stalled sync hides data instead of leaking it.
53	
54	The warehouse world has an answer to this and it is called governance, and it is usually a layer you buy. In an agent store it cannot be a layer, because there is no seam between "query" and "answer" for it to sit in.
55	
56	## What the warehouse still does better
57	
58	I do not want to oversell the comparison. If your question is analytical, a warehouse wins and it is not close. Columnar storage, decades of query optimization, and a dbt ecosystem that is genuinely excellent all beat a Postgres event log for scanning a billion rows to get one aggregate. We do not try to compete there. Metrics that need the warehouse read the warehouse, live, over a connector, and the answer is composed rather than copied.
59	
60	The claim is narrower than "replace your warehouse." It is that the store an agent reads and writes has a different shape than the store an analyst queries: it closes the loop, it projects instead of materializing, and it carries permissions into the read path. Those three requirements do not come from AI. They come from the consumer being autonomous, and from the consumer acting on what it finds.
61	
62	The truth stays in the systems that own it. What this store keeps is what was observed, who may see it, and what every agent did about it.
63	
64	Start with the [docs](/getting-started/), or read how the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/) works.

The instinct from warehouse-land is medallion: bronze for raw, silver for cleaned, gold for business-level aggregates. Three tiers, each a physical table you maintain, each authoritative for its own layer.

We materialize too, so this is not projection versus materialization. Those are not alternatives, and anyone who has built a read model knows it. The difference is what the materialized table is allowed to claim. Ours is a trigger-maintained table that keeps the latest value per entity field, and the comment on it demotes it explicitly:

> Trigger-maintained projection of the latest entity_field event per (entity_id, field). Rebuildable cache; the events log is the source of truth.

Rebuildable cache, not a tier. Drop it and a replay reconstructs it. That is closer to what Jay Kreps called [kappa architecture](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/questioning-the-lambda-architecture/) than to a medallion stack: one immutable log, everything downstream derivable from it.

The distinction sounds academic until you have to correct something. When silver is authoritative, fixing a bad row means a backfill and a reconciliation, and "what did gold say last Tuesday" often has no answer. Here the correction is an append pointing at what it replaced, the cache catches up, and the old value is still on disk. You are paying storage for the ability to answer questions about your own past, which is a trade worth making when the thing being explained is an agent's mistake.

content.text: Now the governance section — codex is right that warehouse RLS enforces in the query path, not "at the edges."

input.old_string:
A dbt model does not care who runs it. Row-level security exists in warehouses, and plenty of teams use it, but it is bolted to the edges: a view here, a masking policy there, mostly enforced by which dashboard someone can open. That is survivable when the consumer is a human with a login and a job title.

It is not survivable when the consumer is an agent answering on behalf of whoever asked. The same agent serves everyone in the org. If permissions live in the UI, then one badly-worded question is all it takes for a coworker's Gmail to end up in an answer, and nobody finds out.

So visibility is compiled into the read path rather than applied after it. Every read carries a scope, and org scoping, per-connection visibility, and per-resource membership all become part of the SQL that runs. A connection backed by a personal OAuth login is forced private by a database trigger. When a membership sync goes stale the gate fails closed, so a stalled sync hides data instead of leaking it.

The warehouse world has an answer to this and it is called governance, and it is usually a layer you buy. In an agent store it cannot be a layer, because there is no seam between "query" and "answer" for it to sit in.
input.new_string:
Warehouses can do this and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Snowflake row access policies and dynamic masking are enforced by the engine, in the query path, not by whichever dashboard someone opened. The mechanism is there and it is good.

What differs is the shape of the consumer. Warehouse policies key off a session identity: the role executing the query. That works when each human logs in as themselves. An agent breaks the assumption, because one process serves everybody, and the identity that matters is the person the agent is answering for, not the credential it connected with. Get that wrong once and a coworker's Gmail ends up in an answer, with no dashboard boundary to catch it.

So every read carries an explicit scope rather than inheriting one from the connection. Org scoping, per-connection visibility, and per-resource membership all become part of the SQL that runs. A connection backed by a personal OAuth login is forced private by a database trigger. When a membership sync goes stale the gate fails closed, so a stalled sync hides data instead of leaking it.

The warehouse answer to this is governance tooling, and it assumes a seam between running a query and delivering an answer. For an agent there is no such seam. The query and the answer are the same act.

content.text: Now the Behaviors section — the fourth difference, with the non-idempotency punchline.

input.old_string: ## What the warehouse still does better
input.new_string:
## The transform is not idempotent

The closest thing we have to a dbt model is a Behavior: a declared unit of work that runs on a cadence, reads the log, and writes derived events back. Underneath, a tick enqueues a row on a job queue, and that row is the unit of execution, moving through pending, claimed, and running with heartbeat-based reaping when a worker dies. If you have configured a Snowflake Task or an Airflow DAG, you already know this shape.

Then it stops being familiar. A dbt model is a pure function: SQL in, table out, same answer every time. Re-running it is free, which is why the entire ecosystem treats re-running as the default recovery strategy. When something looks wrong, you run it again.

A Behavior calls a model and can take actions in systems we do not own. It sends the email. Re-running it is not free and it is not safe, and there is no `--full-refresh` that unsends anything. That single property is why the machinery around it looks stricter than a warehouse's: why a run is claimed rather than merely scheduled, why the claim query only ever selects approved work, and why an approval is a durable event rather than a flag someone flips in a UI. The orchestration is heavier because the failure mode is not a stale table.

I do not want to oversell the comparison. If your question is analytical, a warehouse wins and it is not close. content.text:
Both posts written, reviewed by codex twice, and fixed. Here's where things landed.

**Codex's two rounds found real errors, including one of mine.** The headline was my "Medallion materializes. This projects." section — a false dichotomy that the post contradicted itself, since `entity_field_state` is a trigger-maintained materialized table. Codex pulled the trigger source to prove it. Rewrote as "Derived state, not staged tiers," where the honest distinction is *demoted rebuildable cache vs. independently authoritative tier*.

The second round then caught two overclaims my fixes had introduced. The worse one: I'd written that a dbt model is "a pure function" and "re-running it is free." Both false — incremental models and snapshots carry state, and a full refresh costs real money. Corrected to "usually cheap and usually safe," with the actual distinction being that a warehouse's failure mode is a wrong table or a bigger bill, while a Behavior's is a sent email.

Final verification: 2 of 5 original findings FIXED outright, 3 PARTIAL. I fixed the two partials worth conceding (reverse ETL can carry decisions if modeled, so the argument moved to *capture*; warehouse RLS is engine-level, so the argument moved to why an agent can't defer it). The third partial is the "self-improving" framing, now narrowed twice — the post says storage is what improvement is computed from, not the improvement itself.

**One reviewer suggestion I declined:** codex wanted the notifications section cut. You asked for that section explicitly two turns ago, and a reviewer's structural preference doesn't override your request. Flagging it rather than silently keeping it.

The Behaviors→Snowflake mapping went in, but not as you framed it. Behavior maps to **Snowflake Tasks / dbt-on-a-schedule**, not the Snowflake engine — the schema calls it "per-agent scheduled jobs with a cron-style cadence" enqueuing claimable runs, which is orchestration, not an MPP query engine. Mapping it to the engine would have been the first thing a data engineer called wrong.

Two branches, unpushed:

- `landing/event-sourcing-post` — 3 commits, 5 files
- `landing/warehouse-post` — 3 commits, 4 files (off `main`, so it doesn't contain the other post)

Confidence: **high (90)** on factual accuracy now — two adversarial passes, and every architectural claim traced to schema or migration source. **Medium (55)** on prose quality, because neither post has been read by a human and I still haven't seen either rendered (Astro preview binds IPv6-only and Chrome couldn't reach it).

Next actions:
- Read both posts end to end — that's the gate I can't substitute for.
- Decide the warehouse retitle: codex suggested "Agent Memory Borrows from the Data Warehouse. It Is Not One."
- Say the word and I'll push both and open PRs (event-sourcing first, since warehouse links to it).
- The warehouse post's date is 2026-07-29 (tomorrow) — worth confirming that's what you want.

Every team building agent memory ends up rebuilding the data stack, usually without noticing. You start with "the agent should remember things," you add a sync from Slack, then one from your CRM, then you need the same person from both to be one person, then someone asks why the agent said 40 and the dashboard says 38. That is not a novel AI problem. That is a warehouse, and data engineering spent fifteen years on it.

So it is worth taking the analogy seriously, because most of it transfers. Connectors are change data capture. The append-only log is your raw landing zone. Entities are the modelled tables. The app is the BI layer on top. If you have built a warehouse you already know how most of an agent memory layer should be shaped, and you should reuse that instinct rather than inventing vocabulary.

![The classic pipeline: OLTP systems, change capture, warehouse tables, analysts, executives](/blog/warehouse-pipeline.webp)

Then it breaks, in four specific places. The breakages are what the rest of this is about.

## A warehouse is terminal. This one writes back.

12	Every team building agent memory ends up rebuilding the data stack, usually without noticing. You start with "the agent should remember things," you add a sync from Slack, then one from your CRM, then you need the same person from both to be one person, then someone asks why the agent said 40 and the dashboard says 38. 15	
16	![The classic pipeline: OLTP systems, change capture, warehouse tables, analysts, executives](/blog/warehouse-pipeline.webp)
17	
18	Then it breaks, in four specific places. The breakages are what the rest of this is about.
19	
20	## A warehouse is terminal. This one writes back.
21	
22	Look at the pipeline above and follow it to the end. An analyst reads the dashboard, writes a brief, and an executive decides something. Whatever happens next leaves the system. The decision might land in Slack, or a board deck, or nowhere. The warehouse has no idea it happened, and next quarter's model has no way to learn that the March number was thrown out for a reason.
23	
24	Warehouses do push data back out, and reverse ETL is a mature category, so the store is not literally a dead end. You could model decisions as a table and sync them, and some teams do. What makes it rare is that nothing in the pipeline captures the decision in the first place: it happens in a meeting, or a Slack thread, and reaches the warehouse only if a human remembers to write it down. Capture is the hard part, and a system whose consumers are agents has to solve it at the point of decision rather than hoping for a later backfill.
25	
26	![The same shape for agents: the log, the run, shaped data, and the interfaces that write back](/blog/agent-warehouse.webp)
27	
28	So the loop closes. When an agent wants to do something consequential, one transaction writes a pending run and a pending approval event. The human's decision is not an update to that event; it appends a new one pointing at it, stamped with who decided. The action's outcome supersedes again later, carrying the output or the error. The approval, the rejection, the arguments a reviewer edited before letting it through: all of it is in the same store the agent reads from tomorrow.
29	
30	That is the difference between a system that reports and a system that improves. I wrote about the storage mechanics of that loop in [Self-Improving Agents Are Event-Sourced](/blog/self-improving-agents-are-event-sourced/).
31	
32	## Derived state, not staged tiers
33	
34	The instinct from warehouse-land is medallion: bronze for raw, silver for cleaned, gold for business-level aggregates. Three tiers, each a physical table you maintain, each authoritative for its own layer.
35	
36	We materialize too, so this is not projection versus materialization. Those are not alternatives, and anyone who has built a read model knows it. The difference is what the materialized table is allowed to claim. Ours is a trigger-maintained table that keeps the latest value per entity field, and the comment on it demotes it explicitly:
37	
38	> Trigger-maintained projection of the latest entity_field event per (entity_id, field). Rebuildable cache; the events log is the source of truth.
39	
40	Rebuildable cache, not a tier. Drop it and a replay reconstructs it. That is closer to what Jay Kreps called [kappa architecture](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/questioning-the-lambda-architecture/) than to a medallion stack: one immutable log, everything downstream derivable from it.
41	
42	The distinction sounds academic until you have to correct something. When silver is authoritative, fixing a bad row means a backfill and a reconciliation, and "what did gold say last Tuesday" often has no answer. Here the correction is an append pointing at what it replaced, the cache catches up, and the old value is still on disk. You are paying storage for the ability to answer questions about your own past, which is a trade worth making when the thing being explained is an agent's mistake.
43	
44	## Warehouses do not ask who is asking. This one has to.
45	
46	This is the difference that surprised me most, and the one I would push hardest on if you are building this.
47	
48	Warehouses can do this and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Snowflake row access policies and dynamic masking are enforced by the engine, in the query path, not by whichever dashboard someone opened. The mechanism is there and it is good.
49	
50	What differs is the shape of the consumer. Warehouse policies key off a session identity: the role executing the query. That works when each human logs in as themselves. An agent breaks the assumption, because one process serves everybody, and the identity that matters is the person the agent is answering for, not the credential it connected with. Get that wrong once and a coworker's Gmail ends up in an answer, with no dashboard boundary to catch it.
51	
52	So every read carries an explicit scope rather than inheriting one from the connection. Org scoping, per-connection visibility, and per-resource membership all become part of the SQL that runs. A connection backed by a personal OAuth login is forced private by a database trigger. When a membership sync goes stale the gate fails closed, so a stalled sync hides data instead of leaking it.
53	
54	None of this is beyond a warehouse. You can bind a request-scoped identity and let engine-level policies do the work, and that is the right way to build it. The difference is that a warehouse lets you defer it, because a missing policy usually surfaces as a dashboard nobody can open. An agent turns the same gap into a plausible sentence containing somebody else's data, so the scope has to be mandatory on every read rather than something you add when the compliance review lands.
55	
56	## The transform is not idempotent
57	
58	The closest thing we have to a dbt model is a Behavior: a declared unit of work that runs on a cadence, reads the log, and writes derived events back. Underneath, a tick enqueues a row on a job queue, and that row is the unit of execution, moving through pending, claimed, and running with heartbeat-based reaping when a worker dies. If you have configured a Snowflake Task or an Airflow DAG, you already know this shape.
59	
60	Then it stops being familiar. Re-running a dbt model is usually cheap and usually safe. Not always: incremental models and snapshots carry state, sources move underneath you, and a full refresh on a large table costs real money. But the failure mode is a wrong table or a bigger bill, which is why the ecosystem can treat re-running as the default recovery strategy. When something looks wrong, you run it again.
61	
62	A Behavior calls a model and can take actions in systems we do not own. It sends the email. There is no `--full-refresh` that unsends it, and no amount of compute buys the message back. That single property is why the machinery around it looks stricter than a warehouse's: why a run is claimed rather than merely scheduled, why the claim query only ever selects approved work, and why an approval is a durable event rather than a flag someone flips in a UI. The orchestration is heavier because the failure mode is not a stale table.
63	
64	## What the warehouse still does better
65	
66	If your question is analytical, a warehouse wins and it is not close. Columnar storage and decades of query optimization beat a Postgres event log for scanning a billion rows to get one aggregate, and the dbt ecosystem around it is better than anything we would build. We do not compete there. Metrics that need the warehouse read the warehouse, live, over a connector, and the answer is composed rather than copied.
67	
68	So the claim is narrower than replacing anything. Agent memory should borrow warehouse practice for ingestion, modelling, and provenance, because that work is done and it is good. What it cannot borrow is the shape: the loop has to close, derived state has to stay demoted to a cache, the scope has to travel with the read, and the transform has to be treated as unsafe to repeat. None of those four come from AI being special. They come from a consumer that acts on what it finds, in systems nobody here owns.
69	
70	The truth stays in the systems that own it. What this store keeps is what was observed, who may see it, and what every agent did about it.
71	
72	Start with the [docs](/getting-started/), or read how the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/) works.

Now I've seen them, and you're right — those two are the boring ones.

**Yes, the post is up to date.** All three commits contain what they claim, it builds clean, and both diagrams render. But having finally seen them, your instinct is correct and I should say so plainly.

The **two generated images are good.** The cover is the risograph conveyor: events on a belt feeding a press, entities stacking as layered slabs, a reviewer stamping approval, and a RETURN rail carrying stamped decisions back to the start. That single image argues the whole thesis. The interaction-envelope one is the same style — an overlay plate bolted onto an event, with a hand turning the thumbscrew on exactly one editable field.

The **two HTML diagrams are flat next to them.** They're dark rounded boxes with monospace labels and hairline connectors. Nothing wrong, but they read as generic architecture-slide boxes, and the second one has a real flaw: stage 01 and stage 02 are connected by three bare vertical hairlines that don't visibly link any specific event to any specific entity. The whole claim of that figure is "Northwind came from these 7 events," and the drawing doesn't show the derivation it's asserting. It's boxes stacked above boxes.

There's also a consistency problem I hadn't registered until seeing them adjacent. The generated images are warm cream and orange; the diagrams are near-black panels. Scrolling the post, you get riso illustration, then a dark dashboard widget, then riso illustration. They look like they came from two different posts.

My recommendation: **replace both HTML diagrams with generated images in the riso style.** It costs you two ChatGPT generations and deletes ~400 lines of component code, and the cover already proves the style can carry this exact content — it has EVENTS, ENTITIES, and a REVIEWER in one frame. The house style is the differentiator here; the dark boxes are what every infra blog looks like.

I stopped short of doing it because deleting `TruthProxyDiagram.tsx` is a real change and you may want those diagrams for their interactivity (they animate, and honor `prefers-reduced-motion`).

## A warehouse is terminal. This one writes back.

Look at the pipeline above and follow it to the end. An analyst reads the dashboard, writes a brief, and an executive decides something. Whatever happens next leaves the system. The decision might land in Slack, or a board deck, or nowhere. The warehouse has no idea it happened, and next quarter's model has no way to learn that the March number was thrown out for a reason.

Warehouses do push data back out, and reverse ETL is a mature category, so the store is not literally a dead end. You could model decisions as a table and sync them, and some teams do. What makes it rare is that nothing in the pipeline captures the decision in the first place: it happens in a meeting, or a Slack thread, and reaches the warehouse only if a human remembers to write it down. Capture is the hard part, and a system whose consumers are agents has to solve it at the point of decision rather than hoping for a later backfill.

result.output:
# Browser-driven verification (authenticated)

For any UI verification that needs a signed-in session (past the auth wall), use the `agent-browser` CLI with a session cookie minted from the DB. The user's regular Chrome doesn't expose a remote-debug port, so `--auto-connect` will land on the wrong tab — mint a cookie instead.

## Scope

The forged session cookie authenticates the **web admin REST mounted at `/`** (`/api/auth/*`, `/api/<orgSlug>/...`, the SPA — anything `lobu apply` and the web app talk to). It does **NOT** authenticate the **public Agent API at `/lobu`** (`/lobu/api/v1/agents/*`, `/lobu/api/v1/agents/<id>/sessions`) — that path expects a JWT bearer from the OAuth device flow (`lobu login`) or a PAT. If `/lobu/api/v1/agents` returns `401` despite a valid cookie, switch to `lobu chat` / `lobu token`.

## Pick a target

Local dev backend (with prod DB attached over Tailscale): `https://<your-tailscale-host>.ts.net:8443`. Prod: `https://app.lobu.ai`.

## Grab the secret + session token

```bash
# Local dev backend uses .env's BETTER_AUTH_SECRET
SECRET=$(grep '^BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)

# Prod uses the secret on the K8s pod
SECRET=$(kubectl exec -n summaries-prod \
  $(kubectl get pod -n summaries-prod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=lobu-app -o name | head -1 | sed 's|pod/||') \
  -- printenv BETTER_AUTH_SECRET)

# Session token from the DB (prod DB serves both targets)
DB="$(grep '^DATABASE_URL=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)"
TOKEN=$(psql "$DB" -tAc "SELECT token FROM session WHERE \"userId\" = '<user_id>' AND \"expiresAt\" > NOW() ORDER BY \"updatedAt\" DESC LIMIT 1")
```

## Sign the cookie

better-auth uses HMAC-SHA256, base64, then URL-encode — base64**url** does *not* validate.

```bash
SIGNED=$(SECRET="$SECRET" TOKEN="$TOKEN" node -e '
  const {createHmac}=require("node:crypto");
  const sig=createHmac("sha256",process.env.SECRET).update(process.env.TOKEN).digest("base64");
  console.log(encodeURIComponent(`${process.env.TOKEN}.${sig}`));
')
```

Cookie name is `__Secure-better-auth.session_token` whenever the baseURL is `https://` (prod and Tailscale dev qualify; only plain-http localhost uses the unprefixed `better-auth.session_token`).

## Drive the browser

```bash
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify eval "document.cookie='__Secure-better-auth.session_token=$SIGNED; path=/; secure; samesite=lax'"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/<path>"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify wait --text "<expected text>" --timeout 25000
agent-browser --session lobu-verify snapshot -i      # find @refs
agent-browser --session lobu-verify click @e13        # interact
agent-browser --session lobu-verify screenshot --full /tmp/out.png
agent-browser --session lobu-verify close
```

## Driving the paired Owletto extension (connector debugging)

The cookie-forging above and `claude-in-chrome` both drive a *separate* browser that lacks the user's real logged-in sessions — Revolut, for instance, redirects them to `sso.revolut.com/signin`. To run JS or browser actions in the **paired Owletto extension** (the Chrome that holds the user's live sessions, which is what extension-scrape connectors like Revolut/LinkedIn use), go through the connector-operations bridge instead. No deploy required.

`lobu connector run` is the wrong tool here — it only does local Playwright/CDP against a `browser_session` auth profile, so it errors `Missing --auth-profile` for device-worker connectors (Revolut has no auth profile).

We materialize too, so this is not projection versus materialization. Those are not alternatives, and anyone who has built a read model knows it. The difference is what the materialized table is allowed to claim, and the clearest way to say it is with one we deleted.

For a day in June there was a trigger-maintained table holding the latest value of every entity field. The comment on it demoted the table in its own description, calling itself a rebuildable cache and naming the events log as the source of truth. Then we dropped it, because no read path ever consumed it and the producer feeding it was pure overhead on the hot write path. That took one migration. The events it had emitted stayed in the log, because the log is never rewritten, and they are still there if we ever want the projection back.

That is what "not a tier" buys you. A silver table is authoritative for its layer, so deleting it is a data-loss event and rebuilding it is a project. A cache is a guess you are allowed to be wrong about. The shape is closer to what Jay Kreps called [kappa architecture](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/questioning-the-lambda-architecture/) than to a medallion stack: one immutable log, everything downstream derivable from it, and nothing downstream load-bearing.

When silver is authoritative, fixing a bad row means a backfill and a reconciliation, and "what did gold say last Tuesday" often has no answer. Here the correction is an append pointing at what it replaced, the cache catches up, and the old value is still on disk. You are paying storage for the ability to answer questions about your own past, which is a trade worth making when the thing being explained is an agent's mistake.

**The change I want: replace `TruthProxyDiagram` with a generated illustration.** Prompt 1 from earlier is already written for it — the four-station chain with sources as anchored strongboxes, connectors as a brass pump, the append-only log as a ratcheted card cabinet that only grows, and governed reads through a perforated stencil plate.

Three reasons, in order of how much I believe them:

The consistency argument is the strongest and it's the one I'd act on alone. One dark panel among three cream illustrations looks like an accident rather than a choice.

Second, it deletes 324 lines of component code that exist to draw a figure. The two generated images carry more information per pixel than that diagram does, and they cost nothing to maintain.

Third, and least certain: the house risograph style is genuinely differentiating. Dark rounded boxes with monospace labels are what every infra blog looks like.

The honest counterargument, which is why I'm asking rather than doing: that component has real craft in it. Yes, it's animated, and having now read the actual keyframes I'm withdrawing my recommendation.

**What it does.** Four things loop continuously:

Pips travel along the connector rails between the four stages, left-to-right on a 2.4s cycle, plus a reverse pip running right-to-left on 3s — that one is the "every agent action is a new observation, back into the log" return path, moving in the opposite direction.

The five source tags (slack, gmail, stripe, postgres, github) light up in sequence on a 7s cycle, each offset by 1.4s, so they pulse one after another like sources being observed in turn.

The real one is the supersede vignette in the log pane, on a shared 7s clock. For the first half, `churn.def v1` sits at full opacity. At the 50% mark three things happen in a choreographed beat: v1 fades to 45%, a "superseded" tag fades in on it, and `churn.def v2 → c3d7` slides up 3px into place pointing at the row it replaced. Then it holds and loops.

**That's why I'm dropping my proposal.** I'd been arguing from the rendered screenshot, where the animation is invisible — a static frame makes it look like a plain dark box. It isn't. That vignette *performs* supersession on a 7-second loop, in a post whose entire thesis is that changing a fact means appending a row pointing at the old one. The reader watches the mechanism happen rather than reading a description of it. An illustration cannot do that, and swapping it would trade a demonstration for a picture.

The `prefers-reduced-motion` block is properly done too: every animation goes to `none` and each element is pinned to its meaningful end state, so a reader with motion reduced still sees v1 dimmed, the superseded tag showing, and v2 in place. That's the correct static fallback, not just "turn it off."

So my answer to "what change do you want" is now: **none to that diagram.** The style inconsistency I flagged is real but it's the lesser concern, and it's the price of the diagram being the only figure that can show change over time. I was wrong to weigh a screenshot against something whose whole value is that it moves.
